concepts.name: Constitutional Basis of Judicial Review in India
key_dimensions: Articles 13, 32, 131–136, 143, 226 as textual anchors — no single explicit provision unlike the US
Implied vs. explicit basis: contrast with Article III of the US Constitution
Dr. B.R. Ambedkar's stance in Constituent Assembly debates — Article 32 as 'heart and soul'
UPSC trap: Judicial review is NOT expressly mentioned in the Constitution; it is inferred from multiple articles

concepts.name: Article 13 and the Doctrine of Void Ab Initio
key_dimensions: Article 13(1) vs. 13(2): pre-constitutional vs. post-constitutional laws — 'void' vs. 'shall not make'
Definition of 'law' under Article 13(3): includes ordinances, orders, bye-laws, rules, regulations, notifications — UPSC frequently tests what is included/excluded
Doctrine of eclipse (pre-constitutional laws) vs. doctrine of severability (post-constitutional laws)
UPSC trap: A constitutional amendment is NOT 'law' under Article 13 — until Kesavananda Bharati introduced the Basic Structure doctrine

concepts.name: Scope of Judicial Review: Procedural vs. Substantive Review
key_dimensions: Procedural review: whether law follows prescribed legislative procedure (Articles 107–111, 196–201)
Substantive review: whether content of law violates Fundamental Rights or Basic Structure
India's position: broader than UK (parliamentary sovereignty) but narrower than US (full substantive due process)

UPSC trap: India does NOT follow 'due process of law' (struck from Draft Article 15); uses 'procedure established by law' — yet courts have read due process elements via Articles 14 and 21 post-Maneka Gandhi

concepts.name: Basic Structure Doctrine: Origin, Elements, and Limits on Parliamentary Power
key_dimensions: Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973): 13-judge bench, 7:6 majority — Parliament can amend but not destroy the Constitution
Identified elements: supremacy of Constitution, republican and democratic form, secular character, separation of powers, federal character, judicial review itself
Indira Gandhi v. Raj Narain (1975) and Minerva Mills (1980): consolidation and extension of doctrine
UPSC trap: Basic Structure applies ONLY to constitutional amendments (Article 368), NOT to ordinary legislation — ordinary laws are tested against Part III directly

concepts.name: Judicial Review of Constitutional Amendments (Article 368)
key_dimensions: Shankari Prasad (1951) and Sajjan Singh (1965): amendments not 'law' under Article 13 — Parliament supreme
Golaknath (1967): reversed; amendments ARE law — prospective overruling introduced for the first time in India
Kesavananda Bharati (1973): overruled Golaknath but introduced Basic Structure as the limiting principle
UPSC trap: The 24th Amendment (1971) was Parliament's direct response to Golaknath — tested for sequencing questions

concepts.name: Judicial Review of Ninth Schedule Laws
key_dimensions: Original intent: Articles 31A, 31B, Ninth Schedule to protect land reform laws from judicial scrutiny

I.R. Coelho v. State of Tamil Nadu (2007): 9-judge bench ruled that laws inserted in Ninth Schedule after April 24, 1973 (Kesavananda date) ARE subject to judicial review if they violate Basic Structure or abridge Fundamental Rights under Articles 14, 19, 21
Laws inserted before April 24, 1973 enjoy absolute immunity
UPSC trap: Ninth Schedule does NOT provide blanket immunity — the date of insertion is the critical variable

concepts.name: Writs as Instruments of Judicial Review: Scope and Comparative Jurisdiction
key_dimensions: Article 32 (Supreme Court) vs. Article 226 (High Courts): Article 226 is wider — extends to 'any person or authority' including non-state actors and for purposes other than Fundamental Rights enforcement
Five writs: Habeas Corpus, Mandamus, Prohibition, Certiorari, Quo Warranto — UPSC tests against whom each lies and when
Article 32 is itself a Fundamental Right (cannot be suspended except under Article 359 during Emergency) — Article 226 is not a Fundamental Right
UPSC trap: Habeas Corpus can be issued against private individuals; Mandamus does NOT lie against the President/Governor in personal capacity or purely private bodies

concepts.name: Judicial Review of Executive Action: Grounds and Limits
key_dimensions: Classical grounds: illegality, irrationality (Wednesbury unreasonableness), procedural impropriety — adopted from UK in Indian administrative law
Proportionality review: increasingly adopted post-Modern Dental College (2016) and Puttaswamy (2017) — especially for rights-restricting executive action
Limitations: courts do not substitute their judgment on policy matters; doctrine of deference in national security/foreign affairs (Bihar v. Union of India)

UPSC trap: Courts can review Presidential/Gubernatorial decisions (Rameshwar Prasad v. Union of India on Governor's role in government formation) but cannot direct exercise of discretion in a particular way

concepts.name: Judicial Review of Delegated Legislation
key_dimensions: Two grounds: ultra vires the parent Act (substantive ultra vires) and violation of Fundamental Rights
Procedural ultra vires: failure to follow mandatory consultation, laying before Parliament, etc.
Essential legislative functions cannot be delegated — In Re Delhi Laws Act (1951): foundational case on permissible delegation
UPSC trap: Indian Constitution has no explicit 'non-delegation doctrine' unlike the US — Indian courts apply 'excessive delegation' test more permissively

concepts.name: Doctrine of Severability and the Blue Pencil Rule
key_dimensions: If a part of a statute is unconstitutional, only that part is struck down IF it is severable from the rest — R.M.D. Chamarbaugwala v. Union of India
Test: Would legislature have enacted the valid part alone? Legislative intent is central
Blue pencil rule: court can literally strike out words to save a provision — but cannot rewrite or add words
UPSC trap: Severability vs. Doctrine of Eclipse — Eclipse applies only to pre-constitutional laws; if a post-constitutional law is void, it is void from inception (not merely eclipsed)

concepts.name: Doctrine of Eclipse: Scope and Revival of Pre-Constitutional Laws
key_dimensions: Bhikaji Narain Dhakras v. State of MP (1955): pre-constitutional law inconsistent with Part III is not dead but merely eclipsed — can revive if the inconsistency is removed (e.g., by constitutional amendment)
Applies ONLY to pre-constitutional laws, NOT post-constitutional laws
Revival mechanism: amendment to Part III that removes the inconsistency automatically revives the eclipsed law
UPSC trap: A post-constitutional law that violates Fundamental Rights is void ab initio and CANNOT revive — key distinction

concepts.name: Limitations on Judicial Review: Political Question Doctrine and Non-Justiciability
key_dimensions: Areas traditionally held non-justiciable: declaration of war, recognition of foreign states, advice tendered by PM to President (Article 74(2))
Article 74(2): Courts cannot inquire into the nature of advice given by Council of Ministers to President — statutory bar on review
Speaker's decisions on disqualification under Tenth Schedule: judicially reviewable (Kihoto Hollohan, 1992) but on limited grounds

UPSC trap: Parliamentary proceedings under Articles 105(2) and 194(2) — members cannot be held liable in any court for anything said in Parliament; this is an absolute bar on judicial review of speech inside Parliament

concepts.name: Judicial Review and the Anti-Defection Law (Tenth Schedule)
key_dimensions: Kihoto Hollohan v. Zachillhu (1992): Speaker's order is final but subject to judicial review on grounds of mala fides, perversity, or violation of natural justice — NOT on merits
Speaker acting as a 'tribunal' — orders are subject to Article 136 (SLP) and Articles 226/227
Nabam Rebia (2016): Speaker cannot decide disqualification petition when a notice for their own removal is pending — judicial intervention to protect integrity of process
UPSC trap: Paragraph 7 of Tenth Schedule (which barred judicial review) was struck down in Kihoto Hollohan as violating Basic Structure — courts will always have residual review power

concepts.name: Judicial Review of Emergency Proclamations
key_dimensions: Article 352: National Emergency — originally non-justiciable (State of Rajasthan v. Union of India, 1977); changed post-44th Amendment

44th Amendment Act (1978): Introduced 'armed rebellion' in place of 'internal disturbance'; requires Cabinet's written advice; both Houses must approve within one month — these are now judicially reviewable procedural requirements
Article 356 (President's Rule): Bommai v. Union of India (1994) — subject to full judicial review; floor test is the constitutional imperative; court can restore dissolved Assembly

UPSC trap: During National Emergency, Article 19 rights are automatically suspended (Article 358) — no court order needed; but Articles 20 and 21 can NEVER be suspended even during Emergency (Article 359 amended by 44th Amendment)

concepts.name: Judicial Review and Fundamental Rights vs. Directive Principles: Harmonisation Jurisprudence
key_dimensions: State of Madras v. Champakam Dorairajan (1951): Fundamental Rights prevail over DPSPs — led to First Constitutional Amendment
25th Amendment introduced Article 31C: laws giving effect to Articles 39(b) and 39(c) cannot be challenged under Articles 14 and 19
Kesavananda Bharati curtailed Article 31C; Minerva Mills (1980) struck down extension of Article 31C to ALL DPSPs as destroying balance (Basic Structure)
UPSC trap: Post-Minerva Mills, only laws implementing Articles 39(b) and 39(c) specifically enjoy Article 31C immunity — NOT all DPSPs

concepts.name: Public Interest Litigation (PIL) as an Expanded Form of Judicial Review
key_dimensions: Relaxation of locus standi: S.P. Gupta v. Union of India (1981) — any public-spirited citizen can approach court for redress of public wrong
Epistolary jurisdiction: court can treat a letter as a writ petition (Sunil Batra case)
Limits imposed by Supreme Court: PIL cannot be used for private interest, publicity interest, or to interfere in policy matters — must involve genuine public wrong

UPSC trap: PIL jurisdiction is a JUDICIAL innovation, not a constitutional provision — it flows from Articles 32 and 226 but is not explicitly mentioned; courts have also started imposing costs on frivolous PILs

concepts.name: Judicial Review vs. Judicial Activism vs. Judicial Overreach: Conceptual Distinctions
key_dimensions: Judicial review: constitutionally mandated power to test validity of laws/actions — core and legitimate
Judicial activism: proactive interpretation to protect rights and fill legislative/executive vacuum — PIL era, Vishaka guidelines
Judicial overreach: when courts cross into legislative or executive domain — directions on policy specifics, monitoring executive functions continuously

UPSC trap: The separation of powers doctrine (part of Basic Structure per Kesavananda) itself limits how far judicial review can go — courts cannot direct Parliament to pass a particular law or direct the executive on the content of policy

concepts.name: Judicial Review of Reservation Policies and the Creamy Layer Doctrine
key_dimensions: Indra Sawhney v. Union of India (1992): 9-judge bench — 50% cap on reservations (not absolute), creamy layer exclusion mandatory for OBCs (not SCs/STs), no reservation in promotions (led to 77th Amendment)
M. Nagaraj (2006): Constitutional validity of reservation in promotions for SCs/STs — state must demonstrate backwardness, inadequate representation, and administrative efficiency; 50% cap applies

Jarnail Singh v. Lachhmi Narain Gupta (2018): overruled quantifiable data requirement from Nagaraj for identifying backwardness of SCs/STs — but 50% cap and creamy layer principle for STs in promotions upheld

UPSC trap: Creamy layer concept applies to OBCs (Indra Sawhney) and has been extended to STs in promotions (Jarnail Singh) — but NOT yet formally mandated for SCs in the same manner; this is an evolving area

concepts.name: Judicial Review of Money Bills and Speaker's Certification (Article 110)
key_dimensions: Article 110: defines Money Bill — only specific matters qualify; Speaker's certification is 'final'
Aadhaar case (Justice K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India, 2018): 4:1 majority upheld Aadhaar Act as Money Bill — minority opinion held certification was a fraud on the Constitution
Rojer Mathew v. South Indian Bank (2019): referred question of judicial review of Speaker's Money Bill certification to a larger bench — currently unsettled

UPSC trap: Article 110(3) says Speaker's decision is 'final' — but post-Kihoto Hollohan logic suggests finality clauses do not completely oust judicial review; the question of whether courts CAN review Money Bill certification is constitutionally live and unresolved

concepts.name: Territorial Scope and Extraterritorial Reach of Judicial Review
key_dimensions: Article 245(1): Parliament may make laws for the whole or any part of India — subject to Constitution; Article 245(2): no law of Parliament is invalid merely because it has extraterritorial operation
Judicial review of extraterritorial laws: Indian courts can review such laws for violation of Fundamental Rights but enforcement may be limited

High Court's territorial jurisdiction under Article 226: a High Court can issue writs only if the cause of action arises OR the respondent is located within its territorial jurisdiction — Ambica Industries v. Commissioner of Central Excise
UPSC trap: Unlike Parliament, a State Legislature CANNOT make laws with extraterritorial operation (Article 245 read with List II) — this is a hard jurisdictional limit judicially enforced
